title: Scheduling unit jobs on three machines
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: OpenAI's theorem (2026) that unit jobs with arbitrary precedence constraints can be scheduled on three identical machines with minimum makespan by a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm: a dynamic program over the polynomially many sets described by Boolean formulas of bounded size, made complete by a hierarchy of schedule intervals cut at separators of shared cutoffs, in which short lists of upsets, flattening at changes of direction and two boundary invariants keep every interval's global description below 500 leaves at every depth.
prerequisites: partial orders, Boolean formulas, and running time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine at the level of counting sequential scans
the course proves every fact about orders, schedules and formulas that it uses

checks.exact_checks: Python (scratch sched_checks.py, 10 Oct 2026). The script builds the hierarchy exactly as the course prescribes on random feasible instances (planted full schedules with 2 to 9 slots, arc densities 0.08 to 0.6): centers by the ideal-first walk, sides normalized by exhaustive lexicographic search, shared-cutoff walks, same and switched list updates with carry, injection, pruning, flattening, the short extension and the switch upset. At every node it checks the separator conditions and the walk (Lemmas 3.1-3.3, Corollary 3.4), the priority orders, edge labels and the root walk, carry and pruning (Lemmas 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 of the fifth lesson), list length and injections, the flattening identity, the extension (agreement on the parent, global downset, at most 21 leaves), the switch upset (upset, covers X, nothing at or before a, ancestor arrangement), entry size at most 25 leaves, (I1), (I2) for every child, (I3) for every child over all reorderings (enumerated when at most 400, else sampled), the global child descriptions on all jobs (high part at most 127 leaves, low part at most 130), cutoff predicates (at most 126), the split descriptions in original time (at most 132), that the gaps between marks are exactly the children, and that the dynamic program run on the hierarchy's sets accepts J. Soundness of the dynamic program: with random families on instances of at most 12 jobs, every accepted set's assembled schedule is a full schedule. Final run: 6,000 instances, 2911230 checks of 72 kinds, 0 problems. Random instances rarely reach the flattening lemma; an instance search that maximizes flattening and list length (sched_fuzz.py, 40 rounds of 200 mutations, 8 to 10 slots) found 8 occurrences, and its saved instance with 10 slots, rechecked with the final script, passes all 1,058 checks. Random and searched instances never produced more than one surviving injection or lists longer than two entries, so the five-entry bound is checked as a bound, not reached. Exercise examples (sched_exercises.py): 18 checks, 0 problems. A first final run reported 60 failures of one cross-check (an alternative search for full schedules); the cause was the check script's cache keyed by Python object ids, reused across instances; after the fix the run above has none.

Differences: the course proves the facts about linear extensions, integer start times and reordering that the paper states briefly; states the one-advance lemma with two nested prefixes so that the shared-cutoff walk follows from it directly; counts leaves with the course's own bounds (entries at most 25, node descriptions at most 257, splits at most 132, below the paper's 40 and 500), and notes that K = 257 already makes the dynamic program complete; splits the argument into eight lessons with exercises and full solutions; says where the number three enters (the definitions and the injection count).
